html:
The Pitjantjatjara are an Aboriginal people of the Central Australian desert, near Uluru. They live mostly in the northwest of South Australia, with country reaching into the Northern Territory and a little into Western Australia. They call themselves Anangu, meaning people.

They are part of the Western Desert cultural bloc, and their speech is a dialect of the Western Desert language, close to that of the Yankunytjatjara and Ngaanyatjarra. In the centuries the map shows, small family groups moved between rockholes and soaks, hunting and gathering. Every part of the land carries stories of the Dreaming, called Tjukurpa.

From the 1930s missions and ration depots drew people in, and the British nuclear tests of the 1950s to the south hit Anangu communities hard.

They then won some of the largest land rights in Australia:

  • 1981: the Pitjantjatjara Land Rights Act gave Anangu title to a vast area of northwest South Australia.
  • 1985: Uluru was handed back to its traditional owners, who leased it back as a national park.

Their language is still widely spoken. See Aboriginal Australian societies for the wider story.
